title: Cost, latency & token management
summary: Measure tokens, pick the right model, cache shared context, and stream responses so your LLM apps stay fast and affordable.
objectives: Explain how tokens drive both the cost and the latency of an LLM request
Count tokens before sending a request and estimate the cost
Choose between Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku based on the job
Cut input cost with prompt caching for repeated context
Reduce perceived latency by streaming responses
Cap output cost with sensible max_tokens and the right effort level

quiz.q: What is the unit you are billed on for an LLM API call?
quiz.why: You pay per input and output token; tokens are chunks of text roughly three-quarters of a word each, and output tokens usually cost more than input.

quiz.q: Input tokens and output tokens are priced the same.
quiz.why: False. Output tokens are typically several times more expensive than input tokens, so capping output length matters a lot for cost.

quiz.q: Which tool gives an accurate token count for a Claude prompt before you send it?
quiz.why: tiktoken is OpenAI's tokenizer and undercounts Claude. Use the count_tokens endpoint, which is model-specific and exact.

quiz.q: You send the same 50KB document as context on hundreds of requests. What single technique most reduces your input cost?
quiz.answer: Prompt caching (cache_control on the shared prefix)
quiz.why: Cached prefix tokens are read at roughly one-tenth of the normal input price, so repeated large context becomes far cheaper after the first request.

quiz.q: Streaming makes a long response cost less money.
quiz.why: False. Streaming does not change token cost; it lowers PERCEIVED latency by showing tokens as they arrive instead of waiting for the whole reply.

quiz.q: Name one way to put a hard ceiling on the cost of a single response.
quiz.answer: Set a sensible max_tokens (and/or lower the effort level)
quiz.why: max_tokens caps how many output tokens can be generated, bounding the most expensive part of the bill; effort tunes how much the model thinks.

body_markdown:
## Why cost and latency matter

When you call an LLM you pay per **token** and you wait for tokens to come back. Tokens are small chunks of text — roughly three-quarters of a word each. Two kinds matter: **input tokens** (your prompt) and **output tokens** (the reply). Output tokens usually cost several times more than input tokens.

As a maths graduate, think of the bill as a simple sum: `input_tokens * input_price + output_tokens * output_price`. Latency tracks the same quantities — more output tokens means a longer wait.

## Count tokens before you send

Don't guess token counts, and don't use `tiktoken` — that's OpenAI's tokenizer and it undercounts Claude. Use the model-specific `count_tokens` endpoint to measure exactly, then multiply by the price.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

result = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": open("report.txt").read()}],
)

print(result.input_tokens)
# Sonnet input is $3 per million tokens:
print(f"Input cost: ${result.input_tokens * 3 / 1_000_000:.4f}")
```

## Pick the right model

You rarely need the most powerful model for every job. Match the model to the task:

- **Haiku** (`claude-haiku-4-5`) — fast and cheap; great for classification and simple extraction.
- **Sonnet** (`claude-sonnet-4-6`) — the everyday balance of speed and intelligence.
- **Opus** (`claude-opus-4-8`) — most capable; use it for hard reasoning and long agentic work.

A classifier on Haiku can be many times cheaper than the same task on Opus, with no loss of quality for that job.

## Cache repeated context

If many requests share a big chunk of context — a document, a long system prompt, a set of examples — cache it. A cached prefix is read at roughly one-tenth of the normal input price.

```python
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system=[{
        "type": "text",
        "text": large_document_text,  # the shared, stable part
        "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},
    }],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise the key points."}],
)

print(response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)  # served cheaply from cache
print(response.usage.input_tokens)             # uncached, full price
```

Caching is a **prefix match**: keep stable content first and put the changing question last, or the cache won't hit.

## Stream to cut perceived latency

Streaming doesn't change the bill, but it makes your app *feel* fast — the user sees words appear instead of staring at a spinner.

```python
with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain gradient descent simply."}],
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)
```

## Cap the output

The most expensive part of a request is the output. Set a sensible `max_tokens` so a runaway reply can't blow your budget, and use a lower **effort** level when you don't need deep reasoning. Your task: take one of your earlier scripts, run `count_tokens` on a typical prompt, and work out its cost per thousand calls.

slides.narration: Welcome back. In this lesson we tackle the practical side of building with large language models: cost and latency. Every call you make costs money and takes time, and both come down to one thing — tokens. By the end you'll know how to measure tokens, pick the right model, cache shared context, and stream responses so your apps stay fast and affordable.

slides.title: It all comes down to tokens
bullets: A token is about three-quarters of a word.
You pay for input tokens and output tokens.
Output tokens usually cost several times more.
More output also means longer waits.
slides.narration: Everything starts with the token. A token is a small chunk of text, roughly three-quarters of a word. You're billed for the tokens you send in, the input, and the tokens that come back, the output. Output is usually several times more expensive than input. And here's the link to latency: the more output tokens the model produces, the longer the user waits. So tokens drive both your bill and your speed.

slides.title: Count before you send
bullets: Don't guess; don't use tiktoken.
count_tokens is model-specific and exact.
Then multiply by the price.
slides.code:
result = client.messages.count_tokens(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": text}],
)
print(result.input_tokens)
slides.narration: Before you send anything, measure it. Don't guess, and please don't reach for tiktoken — that's OpenAI's tokenizer and it undercounts Claude. Instead use the count tokens endpoint, which is specific to the model you'll actually call, so it's exact. Once you have the count, multiply by the price per million tokens and you know your input cost before you've spent a penny.

slides.title: The cost formula
bullets: cost = in * in_price + out * out_price
Prices are quoted per million tokens.
Output dominates, so watch reply length.
slides.narration: As a maths graduate you'll like this: the cost of a request is just a sum. Input tokens times the input price, plus output tokens times the output price. Prices are quoted per million tokens, so divide by a million. Because output is the pricier term and you often can't predict its length, controlling how much the model writes is your biggest lever on cost.

slides.title: Pick the right model
bullets: Haiku: fast and cheap simple tasks.
Sonnet: everyday speed and intelligence.
Opus: hardest reasoning, agentic work.
slides.code:
# classify cheaply
client.messages.create(
    model="claude-haiku-4-5",
    max_tokens=16,
    messages=msgs,
)
slides.narration: You rarely need the most powerful model for every job. Haiku is fast and cheap — perfect for classification and simple extraction. Sonnet is the everyday workhorse, balancing speed and intelligence. Opus is the most capable, for hard reasoning and long agentic tasks. A sentiment classifier on Haiku can be many times cheaper than the same job on Opus, with no real loss in quality. Match the model to the task.

slides.title: Cache repeated context
bullets: Shared prefix? Cache it.
Cached reads are about one-tenth the price.
Keep stable content first, question last.
slides.narration: If many requests share a big chunk of context — a long document, a system prompt, a set of examples — cache it. You add a cache control marker to the shared part, and on later requests those tokens are read at roughly one-tenth of the normal input price. The one rule to remember: caching is a prefix match. Keep the stable content first and put the changing question last, or you'll never get a cache hit.

slides.title: Verify your cache hits
bullets: Check usage.cache_read_input_tokens.
Zero reads means a silent invalidator.
Common culprits: a timestamp or UUID.
slides.narration: Don't just assume caching is working — verify it. The usage object on every response tells you how many tokens were read from the cache and how many were charged at full price. If your cache read tokens stay at zero across repeated requests, something is quietly breaking the prefix — usually a timestamp, a random ID, or unsorted Jason that changes the bytes every time. Find it and move it to the end.

slides.title: Stream for speed
bullets: Streaming doesn't lower the bill.
It lowers perceived latency.
Users see words appear immediately.
slides.code:
with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=msgs,
) as stream:
    for t in stream.text_stream:
        print(t, end="", flush=True)
slides.narration: Streaming is about how fast your app feels, not how much it costs. The token bill is identical whether you stream or not. But instead of the user staring at a spinner while the whole reply is generated, streaming sends the text as it's produced, so words appear straight away. For any chat interface or long reply, stream by default — it transforms the experience for free.

slides.title: Cap the output
bullets: max_tokens bounds the priciest part.
Lower effort when deep thinking isn't needed.
Protects you from runaway replies.
slides.narration: Output is the most expensive part of a request, so put a ceiling on it. Set max tokens to a sensible value and a runaway reply simply can't blow your budget. And when a task doesn't need deep reasoning, lower the effort level so the model spends fewer tokens thinking. Together these two settings give you a hard cap and a soft dial on the most costly part of every call.

bullets: Tokens drive both cost and latency.

slides.narration: Let's recap. Tokens drive both your bill and your speed. Count them before you send, then pick the cheapest model that does the job well. Cache any shared context and check that the cache is actually hitting. Stream to make responses feel fast, and cap your output with max tokens and effort to keep cost under control.
